sections.html:
Florence is the seat of Florence County and a city of 39,899 people, the tenth largest in the state at the 2020 count. It covers 23.49 square miles in the coastal plain of northeastern South Carolina. Health care is the biggest employer base: McLeod Regional Medical Center is the largest employer in the Pee Dee region and MUSC Florence is the third largest.

Interstate 20 ends here and Interstate 95 passes through, with Florence Regional Airport about 2 miles east of downtown. That access matters for owners who manage a sale from another city.

sections.h2: Who bills property tax inside the city limits
sections.html:
Florence County collects real estate and personal property tax for the City of Florence, so you receive one county bill that includes the city's levy. City Council sets the millage by June 30 for the July 1 to June 30 fiscal year.

The Florence County Auditor handles vehicle, watercraft, aircraft and business personal property assessments. Bills go to the owner's last known address, and an owner who receives no bill still owes the tax. Keep the Tax Assessor's Office informed about where mail should go.

County offices are open 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday. The city's property tax payments page explains how the city levy works.

Real estate tax is due by January 15. Section 12-45-180 of state law then adds 3 percent on January 16, another 7 percent on February 2 and another 5 percent on March 17, which reaches 15 percent plus collection costs.

Bills usually go out around October. A deadline that lands on a weekend or holiday generally moves to the next business day. You can pay in person at the county complex, mail a payment to 180 N Irby Street, or use the county's PayStar portal. The city warns against mailing cash, and mailed payments are answered with a receipt by mail.

State law offers a narrow break on title changes. If a house changes hands during the tax year, the notice went to the old owner and the new one got none in time, the treasurer shall waive penalties.

sections.h2: What a seller can do about an assessment
sections.html:
You can object in writing to the assessor within 90 days after the assessment notice is mailed. A notice is required when the assessor raises a value by $1,000 or more, and in a reassessment year notices are due by October 1. If you got no notice, you may appeal in writing at any time, and the appeal applies to the current year only if it is filed before the first penalty date.

The county reassesses every five years, limits a parcel's increase to 15 percent over that period unless an assessable transfer of interest occurs, and rolls back the millage when overall values rise. Appeals go in writing to the Assessor's office, and a PDF form is available. Call the Assessor at 843-665-3056 to learn which cycle and dates apply to you.

sections.h2: If taxes on a Florence house go unpaid
sections.html:
Unpaid real property and mobile home taxes may lead to a public sale run by Florence County. Charges build up first. Recent amounts include $20 for notices in March, $30 for certified mail of a levy in April, $25 for advertising in August and $60 for a land mortgage search in October.

The latest sale was set for October 5, 2026 in the parking garage at the County Complex. The owner or a mortgage holder has one year and a day to redeem, and interest rises at 3, 6, 9 and 12 percent of the bid in quarterly steps. Past-due solid waste fees add $25 if paid after March 16. A tax deed is not a warranty deed, and the county says liens can remain.

sections.h2: Selling a Florence house that owes tax
sections.html:
A balance does not close the door on a sale. Call 843-665-3095 for the payoff figure before you set a closing date, and have your title company include it on the settlement statement.

  1. Get the payoff, since penalties step up in January, February and March and costs rise through the year.
  2. Ask the Assessor to confirm where bills are mailed.
  3. Check the mortgage holder's records if the loan is escrowed.
  4. Ask the City Finance Department at 843-665-3162 how the city's share appears on the bill.

Houses in a city with a long summer rely on their air conditioners, attic ventilation and roofs, and a buyer's inspector will test cooling equipment and look for water stains. Servicing both before you list avoids a surprise in the inspection report.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax for the City of Florence?
faqs.a: Florence County does. The County Treasurer collects City of Florence real estate and personal property taxes on the same county bill.

faqs.q: When is the property tax deadline in Florence, SC?
faqs.a: January 15. A 3 percent penalty starts January 16, and more is added on February 2 and March 17, for 15 percent in total plus costs.

faqs.q: Who sets the city's property tax rate?
faqs.a: City Council sets the millage by June 30 for the July 1 to June 30 fiscal year. You pay it on the county bill.

faqs.q: What if I never received a Florence tax bill?
faqs.a: You still owe the tax. Bills go to the owner's last known address, so keep the Tax Assessor's Office up to date on where mail goes.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Florence house if I owe taxes?
faqs.a: Yes, but the balance and any fees must be cleared. Call the Delinquent Tax Office at 843-665-3095 for a payoff figure before you set a closing date.
